title: Explain any three microservices design patterns in detail (e.g. API Gateway, Circuit Breaker, Database-per-Service).
shortTitle: Three microservices design patterns in detail
keyPoints: API Gateway is the single entry point that handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, and request aggregation.
The gateway hides the internal topology so you can split or rename a service without changing clients.
Circuit Breaker tracks failure rate over a sliding window and flips CLOSED to OPEN to fail fast.
Circuit Breaker is always paired with a timeout and a bulkhead for complete resilience.
Database-per-Service gives each service exclusive ownership of its data store with no shared schema.
These three patterns reinforce each other: DB-per-service forces network calls, network calls need circuit breakers, and the gateway enforces auth for all of them.

s1_definition.oneliner: API Gateway is the single front door, Circuit Breaker fails fast to stop cascades, and Database-per-Service keeps each service's data private so services stay independent.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **API Gateway** – a single entry point handling routing, authentication, rate limiting, and request aggregation so clients never talk to services directly.
- **Circuit Breaker** – wraps remote calls, tracks failure rate over a sliding window, and flips CLOSED to OPEN to fail fast, then HALF_OPEN to test recovery.
- **Database-per-Service** – gives each service exclusive ownership of its data store, so services are decoupled at the data layer and evolve schemas independently.
- **Reinforcement** – these three interlock: DB-per-service forces network calls, network calls need circuit breakers, and the gateway is where you enforce auth and rate limits for all of them.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, the API Gateway is the reception desk that checks your ID, limits how many people enter per minute, and points you to the right department. The Circuit Breaker is the "counter temporarily closed" sign: when the cash desk cannot serve, staff put up the sign so customers do not keep queuing and jamming the lobby. Database-per-Service is giving each department its own private ledger that no other department can open directly; if the loan department wants account data, it must ask the account department, not peek into its books.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When asked to explain microservices patterns in detail, I pick the three that nearly every real system needs and show how they reinforce each other. The API Gateway is the single entry point that handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, and request aggregation, so clients never talk to services directly. At National Bank of India, the mobile app makes one authenticated call to the gateway for Rajesh's dashboard, and the gateway fans out to the account and payment services and merges the responses.

The Circuit Breaker wraps a remote call and tracks the failure rate over a sliding window. When failures cross the threshold it flips from closed to open and every call fails instantly by invoking a fallback. I always pair it with a timeout so a slow call counts as a failure, and a bulkhead so one slow dependency does not consume all threads.

Database-per-Service gives each service exclusive ownership of its data store. The Payment Service owns the payments tables and the Account Service owns the accounts tables, with no shared schema and no cross-service joins. The tradeoff is that you lose cross-service ACID transactions and must use the Saga pattern with eventual consistency.

Remember one sentence: DB-per-Service forces network calls, network calls need Circuit Breakers, and the API Gateway enforces auth and rate limits for all of them in one place.
